summary: This informational document describes features and use cases of an MPLS path monitoring system. Segment-based routing offers a scalable and simple way to check the liveness of all the paths in one domain. The system adds features to traditional MPLS monitoring.

eli5.summary: A security guard walks every corridor to check each is open. This describes a scalable way to do that for a network's paths.

questions: how to monitor mpls data plane liveness
what is a topology-aware mpls monitoring system
what is a path monitoring system in mpls
how does segment routing help mpls monitoring
subtitle: A monitoring server that uses Segment Routing label stacks to send its own probes along chosen MPLS paths and catch them coming back.

tldr.problem: Operators of large MPLS networks need to check that forwarding paths really work in the data plane, and to find where a path breaks, without heavy control-plane involvement.
tldr.mechanism: A Path Monitoring System (PMS) learns the IGP and MPLS topology, then builds a label stack that carries a probe out along the path to be tested and back to itself, so the sender also receives the probe.
tldr.outcome: The document describes the system and its use cases as Informational; it reuses existing OAM protocols, so it introduces no new interoperability considerations.

today: RFC 8403 is an Informational RFC from July 2018, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes a monitoring framework built on RFC 8402 Segment Routing and the OAM tools of RFC 8029, rather than a new protocol.

sections.title: The Idea Behind the Path Monitoring System
sections.content:
Operators need to monitor the forwarding paths that carry user packets, and monitoring packets should be forwarded in the data plane much like user packets. Segment Routing (SR) forwards packets along predefined paths and segments, so an SR monitoring packet can stay in the data plane while it passes along the segments being monitored.

The RFC calls the functional component a Path Monitoring System (PMS). It is limited to a single IGP MPLS domain, may be a physical or virtual node, and can monitor non-SR LSPs such as LDP as well as SR LSPs. Benefits listed include a domain-wide centralized connectivity check, ping packets that never leave the MPLS user data plane, free choice of probe payload, and a flexible deployment from one centralized system to several distributed ones.

The document describes both use cases and a standalone framework. Because it reuses existing IETF OAM protocols, it states there are no new interoperability considerations and that Informational status is appropriate.
sections.eli5: One guard checks the whole building from a single desk by sending probes and watching them come home.

sections.title: How the PMS Builds a Probe
sections.content:
Any node that at least listens to the IGP of an SR domain is MPLS topology aware. A PMS that learns the IGP Link State Database, including the segment identifiers (SIDs), can chain arbitrary LSPs. It only needs to be attached to one router of the domain and to send and receive MPLS packets there; it does not take part in IGP or MPLS routing, and a static route will do.

To test the path from LER i to LER j, the PMS sends a label stack with three parts. The top label is the Node-SID of LER i. The next label is the path to monitor from LER i to LER j, which can be a Node-SID, an Adj-SID for a single interface or bundle, or a list of segments. The last element is the way back to the PMS, usually just popping the stack to reveal a probe addressed to the PMS.

Probes can use ICMP, BFD, Seamless BFD or MPLS LSP ping, or any other OAM format the PMS supports. As long as the probe returns while no IGP change is detected, the monitored path is considered validated.
sections.eli5: The probe carries a list of stops written on it. Each stop tells it where to go next, and the last one sends it home.

sections.title: Worked Use Cases
sections.content:
Use case 1, LSP monitoring. With Node-SIDs PMS = 10, LER i = 20 and LER j = 30, the PMS sends a measurement packet with the label stack (top to bottom) 20 - 30 - 10. The RFC suggests first using an MPLS path trace per RFC 8029 to find IP destination addresses that steer pings along each ECMP path, so that the stack needs no more than 3 labels. Alternatively, a path can be fixed by listing every Node-SID along it, such as 20 - 40 - 30 - 10.

Use case 2, a remote bundle. To test three parallel links between routers R1 and R2, the PMS adds the segment list {72, 662, 992, 664}: to R2 (Node-SID 72), over link L1 to R1, back over L2, then over L3 to R1, which sends the IP probe to the PMS.

Use case 3, fault localization. Two probes, 72, 662, 992, 664 and 72, 663, 992, 664, differ only in the middle link's Adj-SID 663. If the first succeeds and the second fails, the middle link in the R2 to R1 direction is the culprit. The RFC adds that real deployments need well-designed engineering for an unambiguous diagnosis.
sections.eli5: To find a broken corridor among three, the guard sends one car through each variation of the route and compares which ones come back.

sections.title: Verifying Connectivity and Non-SR Networks
sections.content:
A probe that comes back proves continuity, but not that it took the expected path. If a forwarding entry is misprogrammed, a probe can still return and give a falsified liveness indication. For connectivity verification, the PMS can intermittently send a stack such as {40;ttl=255} {30;ttl=1} {10;ttl=255}. The node at the middle label punts the packet when the TTL expires and answers; a wrong node sends a negative response because the Target FEC Stack or Discriminator in the probe does not match it.

For LSPs that are not SR based (LDP, possibly RSVP-TE), the PMS needs another way to learn the MPLS topology, such as management-plane access or a dedicated tLDP tunnel per router, and the IGP must be monitored to avoid stale labels. An SR-based PMS in a mixed network can use SR Node-SIDs to reach and leave the LDP or RSVP-TE LSP being tested. An implementation report on a PMS in an LDP domain is cited; it reports that PMS round-trip delay measurements matched an IPPM-conformant system for 64 Byte packets with 95% confidence.
sections.eli5: A returning car does not prove it took the right corridor. So sometimes the guard makes the car stop and check in at a certain door on the way.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The PMS builds packets from topology information, and it can insert traffic into non-SR domains, which could be abused to inject traffic into external IP domains or MPLS-based VPNs. The RFC suggests reserving label ranges for service labels and having the PMS reject them, and allowing only IP destination addresses that conform to RFC 8029. Access to a PMS needs to be authorized and should be logged, and a tunnel-based connection to an SR domain is not recommended.

Stale topology is the other risk, since it could make a monitoring packet leave the domain it started in. The PMS must respect route changes and SID assignments, stop operations on sections whose topology may be stale, and remove all IGP and MPLS topology information before restarting after a crash. The RFC has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: A guard who can send cars anywhere must be trusted, and must not use an old map, or a car might wander into the wrong building.
